tldr: A recruiter's first pass takes about 7.4 seconds, and the software everybody blames ranks résumés while people reject them, over four specific doubts. A generic application adds a fifth: 62 percent of employers in one survey said AI-generated résumés with no customization are more likely to be rejected.

blocks.text: You get about seven seconds on the first read

A recruiter's first pass over a résumé takes about 7.4 seconds. In the eye-tracking study behind that figure, most of the attention went to job titles, and the résumés that did best had clear section headings and a short overview at the top of page one. The average opening now draws about 242 applications, up 111 percent since 2022, so the first pass is a sort into maybe or no. Everything lower on the page is for the second read, and only the maybe pile gets one. Rewrite the summary, the skills line and the first three bullets under your most recent job before you touch anything else.

items: Print page one of your current résumé and cover everything below the top third with a sheet of paper.
Hand it to someone outside healthcare for seven seconds, then take it back before they can be polite about it.
Ask one question: what job do you think I am applying for?
Count "speech therapist" or a blank look as this week's work, and do that work above the sheet of paper.
Keep the page. Run the same test on the same person after lesson 4.5 and watch what changes.

blocks.text: The software ranks your résumé, and a person rejects it
Any tips how you got through ATS?
blocks.from: an SLP replying to a data analyst who got hired, r/SLPcareertransitions

blocks.text: Applicant tracking systems store, search and rank applications, and recruiters reject them. The claim that 75 percent of résumés are auto-rejected before a human sees them traces to a 2012 sales pitch from a company that sold résumé optimization. In one small survey, about 92 percent of recruiters said they do not auto-reject anyone on a match score. That is heavier news than the robot story, because a person looked at your bullets, could not map them onto the job they were filling, and moved on.

blocks.title: What applicant tracking software does with your résumé

left.label: The story
items: A robot rejects most résumés before anyone reads them.
Keywords hidden in white text get you past the filter.
A designed two-column template helps you stand out.
The résumé is the only thing being screened.

right.label: What happens
items: The system stores, searches and ranks. A recruiter does the rejecting.
Hidden text appears as plain text on the recruiter's screen, and it costs you their trust.
Tables, text boxes and graphics can scramble when the system pulls out your text.
Knockout questions on the form can screen you out: experience, licenses, work authorization, salary.
Use one column and the standard headings: Experience, Skills, Education.
Take out tables, text boxes and graphics.
Use the posting's own words wherever they are true of your work, because recruiters search by them.
Paste the file into a plain-text editor. If the order reads wrong there, the system reads it wrong too.
Answer the knockout questions honestly, and decide your salary number before you open the form.

blocks.text: Four doubts get career changers rejected

items.title: Will you go back?
items.text: Retention doubt. Ten years under one clinical title argues you might return to the clinic the first hard month. Your letter argues against it.

items.title: Clinical words they can't map
items.text: Caseload, IEP, dysphagia protocol, SOAP note, productivity. Each is real work, and none of it means anything to someone hiring for onboarding or quality reporting.

items.title: No proof you have invested
items.text: Nothing on the page cost you anything: no project, no course, no artifact, no sign you have spoken to one person who does this job.

items.title: Salary mismatch
items.text: They assume a master's-level clinician will find their pay band insulting, so they skip the conversation and skip you with it.

blocks.text: Your résumé fixes the second doubt outright and chips at the other three. For the salary doubt, arrive with numbers: median SLP pay is $97,870, and the middle half of the profession earns between $77,730 and $114,570. When a form makes salary a required box, answer from the documented range for your path, and use the SLP band to see how that compares with your pay now. A number decided in advance beats one invented at eleven at night with the posting open in another tab.
A generic application gets cut, whoever wrote it

Hiring managers reject the generic application, and generic is what an AI tool writes by default. In one survey, 62 percent of employers said AI-generated résumés with no customization are more likely to be rejected. In another, 33.5 percent of hiring managers picked the AI-written résumés out of a set, and the ones who did took about 20 seconds. One hiring manager reported that 35 percent of applicants had sent identical AI-generated answers to the same question. A generic letter costs a career changer most, because yours is the application with explaining to do.

blocks.title: What a reader takes for generated text

left.label: Reads as generated
items: Adept, leverage, spearheaded, cutting-edge, results-driven, with no number attached to any of them.
An adjective where a number belongs: "significantly improved outcomes".
The five-paragraph letter: interest, adjectives, flattery, restated résumé, look forward to discussing.

right.label: Reads as yours
items: A plain verb and a count you can defend.
The before and the after, taken from the tracker.
One paragraph about this company that no other applicant could send.

blocks.text: Make the tool interview you, then write the sentences yourself
can you provide the prompts you used for ChatGPT?
blocks.from: an SLP on a transition thread, r/SLPcareertransitions

items: Give it your sentence, your number and the posting, and ask it to rewrite that sentence in the posting's vocabulary. Never ask it to write the bullet from nothing.
Ask it to ask you five questions about the bullet before it rewrites anything, and answer them out loud. The answers are the material.
Paste the posting and ask which of your bullets map to which requirement, and which requirements have no evidence behind them. That gap list is worth more than any prose it hands you.
Feed it a sample of your own writing, an email or a message you sent, so the draft comes back in a voice you can edit.
Keep client names and employer documents out of everything you paste.
Delete every sentence that could appear on another applicant's page unchanged. If a teacher leaving the classroom could send it as written, it does nothing for you.
Read the whole thing aloud, and cut anything you would not say to a colleague standing in front of you.

blocks.title: Generated, then remembered
blocks.before: Adept at leveraging strong communication skills to spearhead results-driven outcomes across diverse stakeholder populations in fast-paced clinical environments.
blocks.after: Rebuilt the referral intake form and the evaluation schedule after the backlog hit [11] weeks, and brought it to [4] weeks in one term without adding staff.

blocks.title: The specifics are the part no model can generate
blocks.text: The tool was not in your IEP meetings. It does not know the caseload hit 62 in March, that you trained 14 people through the EMR switch, or that the front office would only let you touch the note template. Those details are why only you can send your application, and generic output erases them.

items.q: Your résumé is a two-column template with a skills sidebar, and eight applications have brought no replies. What do you fix first?
options: Add the posting's keywords in white text at the bottom of the page.
Rebuild it in one column and rewrite the summary and top three bullets in the posting's words.
Pay for a tool that scores the résumé against the software.
items.why: The software ranks and a person rejects, so the fix is a file that reads cleanly and a top of page one a stranger can map onto the job.

items.q: You ask ChatGPT for a cover letter and it returns five smooth paragraphs. What do you do with them?
options: Send them, since most hiring managers cannot spot AI writing.
Run them through a tool that makes the text sound more human.
Replace every sentence another applicant could send with your own numbers and details.
items.why: A generic application gets cut whoever wrote it, and the details only you have are what make it yours.

blocks.label: Three details only you could write
blocks.prompt: Write three details only you could put in an application: a number, a tool, and something you built.

takeaways: The first pass is about 7.4 seconds and goes mostly to job titles and the top of page one, so rewrite the summary, skills and first three bullets first.
The 75 percent auto-rejection figure comes from a 2012 sales pitch. Systems rank and people reject, and the knockout questions on the application form are the real automatic filter.
Four doubts reject career changers: retention, clinical language nobody can map, no proof of investment, and salary mismatch.
Use an AI tool to interview you, map your bullets against the posting and find your gaps, and write the sentences yourself.
Delete any sentence that could appear unchanged on another applicant's page.

tldr: Translation means describing work you already did in words the reader already knows. Swapping nouns produces word salad. Rebuilding each bullet around how big it was, what you did and what changed gives a hiring manager something to picture.

blocks.text: Swapping the nouns gives you word salad

Almost everybody swaps the nouns first. Caseload becomes portfolio, parents become stakeholders, IEP meetings become cross-functional alignment, and the bullets still list duties with no outcome anywhere. One SLP paid a résumé writer $220 for that swap on the way to a six-figure project management job.
My resume was better beforehand, they just turned it into word salad.
blocks.from: an SLP who became a project manager, r/SLPcareertransitions

blocks.title: The swap, seen in the wild, and the translation
blocks.before: Orchestrated daily end-to-end client workflows for premium accounts, maintaining 100% data compliance.
blocks.after: Ran a caseload of 62 with a plan, a timeline and a quarterly review for each, and finished every note the same day for a year.

blocks.text: The first version could describe a hotel concierge, and a hiring manager cannot picture one day of it. The second names the size, the work and the result in words anyone can check.
Give every bullet a size, an action and a change

items.label: How big it was
items.note: 62 on the caseload, three sites, 48 evaluations a year

items.label: What you did
items.note: a verb from the posting: ran, rebuilt, led, trained

items.label: What changed
items.note: the result: a signed plan, a fixed turnaround, same-day notes

blocks.text: A bullet that answers all three survives the first pass, and one that skips the change reads as a duty. Take the verb from the posting and leave the number exactly where it was. A noun can change too, once the sentence has all three parts. Six good bullets under your most recent role beat fourteen complete ones, because a caseload trains you to account for your time and a résumé accounts for what your time moved.

blocks.title: Trade the verbs of care for the verbs of ownership

left.label: Care given
items: Provided, delivered
Implemented
Facilitated
Assisted with

right.label: Something moved
items: Ran, led
Rebuilt, cut
Negotiated, closed
Trained

blocks.text: Test each bullet by asking whether a colleague down the hall could have written the same line about their own year. "Provided speech-language services across a caseload" is true of every SLP alive, so it is a job description, and it goes.

blocks.title: Caseload, rebuilt
blocks.before: Managed a caseload of 62 students across three schools. Completed evaluations and wrote IEPs.
blocks.after: Managed 62 client accounts at a time across three sites, each with its own goals, timeline and quarterly review, and completed [48] evaluations a year inside a fixed turnaround.

blocks.title: The meeting nobody wants to run
blocks.before: Attended IEP meetings with parents, teachers and administrators.
blocks.after: Led [9] cross-functional meetings a month with families, educators and administrators, negotiating goals between people with competing priorities and closing each one with a written, signed plan.

blocks.text: Keep only the bullets you could talk about for ten minutes

Translation turns into spin at the point where you could not talk for ten minutes about the day behind the bullet, to someone who already does the job you want, without inventing anything. If you can, it is translation, however corporate it sounds out loud. If your stomach moves, take the number down or take the claim out, because everything on the page comes back as an interview question. Write "led" only for the meetings you ran. An accurate bullet can still feel like bragging, because work looks small from the inside once you have done it four hundred times.
I won't lie, I exaggerated my role a lot to where it felt like lying.
blocks.from: an SLP who became a project manager, r/SLPcareertransitions

blocks.title: Your job title stays Speech-Language Pathologist
blocks.text: Employers verify titles and dates, and a renamed title can cost you an offer. Put the translation in a short function line underneath the title: client portfolio, cross-functional program delivery, staff training.

items.q: Your bullet reads "Facilitated cross-functional stakeholder alignment across diverse populations." What fixes it?
options: Swap in stronger business nouns from the posting.
Add how many meetings you led, what you did in them and what each one ended with.
Cut it, because IEP meetings do not count outside a school.
items.why: The bullet has business nouns and no size, action or change, which is the word salad the swap produces.

items.q: A posting asks for program management. You coordinated a caseload of 62 and never held that title. What goes on the résumé?
options: Program Manager as your title, so it matches the posting.
Speech-Language Pathologist as your title, with a function line under it.
The clinical résumé unchanged, with the explanation saved for the letter.
items.why: Employers verify titles, so the title stays and the function line carries the translation.

takeaways: Swapping clinical nouns for business nouns leaves the sentence describing a duty, which is how expensive résumé rewrites turn into word salad.
Every bullet answers three questions in one sentence: how big it was, what you did, what changed.
Pull the verb from the posting and leave the number where it already is.
The honesty test is whether you could talk for ten minutes about the day behind the bullet without inventing anything.
Keep Speech-Language Pathologist as the title and put the translation in a function line underneath it.

tldr: No number, no bullet. You have more numbers than you think, and most were never written down because nobody has ever asked an SLP by how much.

blocks.text: Your ordinary week is already full of numbers

Your ordinary week produces numbers, and almost none of them are on your résumé: 62 on the caseload in March, three buildings, 48 evaluations a year, 14 people trained through the EMR switch, nine IEP meetings in a heavy month. Clinical work is counted constantly, in the IEP tracker, the productivity report and the sign-in sheet from the in-service you ran. Nobody ever asked you to carry those counts over.
companies want numbers - by how much did your project x improve variable y? Which is very hard as an SLP
blocks.from: an SLP moving into data work, r/SLPcareertransitions

blocks.text: You already hold size and rate, and you have to build change

items.title: Size
items.text: The largest caseload you carried, buildings covered, evaluations completed in a year, people trained or supervised, districts or units served.

items.title: Rate
items.text: Anything per week, per month or per quarter: meetings led, sessions delivered, charts reviewed, referrals processed, notes written.

items.title: Change
items.text: A before and an after with your hand in the middle: evaluation backlog, no-show rate, dismissal rate, documentation minutes a day, days from referral to first session.

blocks.text: Companies want the size of a change, and change is the number clinicians rarely have written down. Size and rate are sitting in your calendar. Change you construct, usually from something you fixed and never told anyone about. One client's progress stays off your résumé. What goes on it is what happened to the system around your clients, as totals that identify nobody: how long families waited, how many evaluations cleared, how much of the department's Sunday went to documentation after you rebuilt the template.

blocks.title: The EMR rollout you helped with
blocks.after: Trained [14] clinicians through an EMR transition, built the note templates the department still uses, and tracked documentation time down from [90] to [55] minutes a day.

blocks.title: Chart audits, which are quality assurance
blocks.before: Completed chart audits and peer reviews.
blocks.after: Audited [40] charts a quarter against payer criteria, fed the three most common errors into a 30-minute team training, and cut returned claims from [12] a month to [4].

blocks.text: Go and get your numbers from last year's calendar this week

items: Open last year's calendar, count the IEP meetings or care conferences in three ordinary months, and multiply. That is your rate, and it will be higher than you guessed.
Pull the largest caseload number you carried and note the month, so you can defend it out loud.
Count everyone you trained, supervised or oriented, including CFs, grad students, aides, teachers and the nurses at that one in-service.
Name one thing that got better or worse on your watch, then go find the two numbers on either side of it. A wait time, a backlog, a documentation load, a dismissal rate.
Put [brackets] around anything you cannot verify yet and keep moving. Brackets are a promise to check before you send, and they beat a rounded-up guess you will have to defend in an interview.
Round down when you are unsure. A defensible 55 does more for you than a wobbly 70.

items.q: You remember cutting the evaluation backlog and cannot recall the exact weeks. What goes in the bullet today?
options: Nothing. Leave the bullet out until you can prove the figure.
Your estimate in [brackets], rounded down, to check against the tracker before you send.
Your best guess, rounded up, since nobody will check.
items.why: Brackets are a promise to verify before you send, and a rounded-down number is one you can defend in an interview.

takeaways: No number, no bullet, and estimates you can defend count.
Size and rate are already sitting in your calendar and your caseload. Change is the one you have to construct, out of something you quietly fixed.
Rebuild one number from source instead of from memory, because the interview will ask you where it came from.
Bracket anything unverified and round down when you are unsure.
The numbers you mine here feed the résumé in 4.5 and the bridge statement in Module 6.

tldr: Paste your résumé exactly as it reads today and one real posting into the Suite. It returns every bullet translated against that posting's actual requirements, a cover letter, LinkedIn sections and a list of requirements you have no evidence for. Then you spend twenty minutes making every line true.

blocks.text: The Suite builds your first draft from your résumé and one real posting

The Career Pivot Suite reads your own history against one real posting and translates it by the rules from 4.2 and 4.3, and it is included with the program. It answers the most common request in every SLP exit thread, which is the finished résumé itself. One project manager's post drew more than twenty comments asking for theirs. People rarely share one, because it names their employer and their city.
Would you mind sharing your revamped resume with me?
blocks.from: one of twenty-plus commenters on a single exit post, r/SLPcareertransitions

blocks.title: From clinical résumé to a draft you can send

items.label: Paste
items.note: your résumé as it reads today, and one real posting

items.label: Read the gaps
items.note: requirements with no evidence behind them

items.label: Make it true
items.note: every number checked, every line defensible

blocks.text: Paste your résumé as it reads today, with one real posting

items: Paste your résumé exactly as it reads today, clinical language and all. Translating it first makes the output worse, because the tool needs to see the caseload before it can translate it.
Add one real posting for your path, as text or as a link. A job title or a category is too little, because the match score is built from the requirement lines.
Add the numbers from 4.3, brackets included. A number you leave out cannot appear in the bullets.
Add a short sample of your own writing if you have one, so the cover letter sounds like a person you recognize.
Keep the pair you saved in 4.2 beside you. Every rewritten bullet has to be as true as that one.

blocks.text: Read the list of gaps before you read the new bullets

items.title: Your résumé
items.text: A match score built from the posting's actual requirements, and every bullet rewritten against them.

items.title: Your application
items.text: A tailored cover letter, answers to screening questions, and your answer to "why are you leaving clinical work?" for the same role.

items.title: Your LinkedIn
items.text: A headline and an About section, which lesson 3.4 checks against.

items.title: Your gaps and plan
items.text: What the job wants that you don't show yet, one thing to build that proves you can do the work, a 90-day plan, and editable Word documents.

blocks.text: Read the requirements coverage first, even though most people skim it. Every requirement with no evidence behind it is either a bullet you forgot to write or a real gap, and telling the two apart takes about five minutes. The forgotten ones go back into the résumé this week. The real ones become your list for Module 5.
Spend your ten refinements on specific complaints
You get ten refinements across six sections, which is plenty if each one names a specific complaint. A vague request returns adjectives. A specific one returns the sentence you wanted.

blocks.title: A refinement request
blocks.after: This bullet has no number in it. Use the posting's word onboarding instead of orientation.

blocks.title: Read every line before it goes anywhere
blocks.text: The draft is built from what you pasted, and a rewritten bullet can still claim more than you did. Check every number against its source, and fix anything you could not defend out loud for ten minutes.

items.q: Your résumé is ready to paste. Do you rewrite it in business language before you paste it into the Suite?
options: Yes, so the tool starts from a stronger draft.
No. Paste it exactly as it reads today.
Only the summary at the top.
items.why: The tool needs the clinical version in front of it to translate it against the posting.

items.q: The coverage list says you show no evidence of training end users. You ran the EMR in-service for your department. What is that requirement?
options: A real gap to close in Module 5.
A forgotten bullet to write into the résumé this week.
A reason to pick a different posting.
items.why: You did the work and never wrote it down, so it goes back into the résumé and stays off the gap list.

action.label: I built the first draft
action.prompt: Open the Suite, paste your résumé exactly as it reads today plus one real posting for your path, and run it. Then spend twenty minutes on the output: check every number, delete every sentence that could belong to another applicant, and spend two refinements on the two weakest sections.
action.done: First translation done. Your experience is now legible to someone who has never met an SLP.

takeaways: Paste your résumé untranslated, because the tool needs to see the clinical version before it can translate it.
Use one real posting, because the match score is built from its actual requirement lines and a job title has none.
Read the requirements coverage first and sort the gaps into forgotten bullets and real gaps.
Spend refinements on specific complaints, since "make it stronger" only ever returns adjectives.
Every line has to be one you could defend out loud for ten minutes before it goes anywhere.

tldr: Some recruiters skip the cover letter, and the readers who open it take it as evidence that you spent effort on this company and no other one. Four beats, about 250 words, and one paragraph in the middle that nobody else could have written.

blocks.text: Send a letter even when it is optional, because you have a change to explain

Some recruiters skip cover letters and many hiring managers read them, so write yours for the reader who does. The letter is the one place a career changer can say why an SLP is applying, which a résumé cannot do. That reader judges it on effort before prose, and a letter that could go to eighty companies before lunch shows none. Ten minutes of research and one honest paragraph is effort a reader can see.
Write about where you are going, and leave out what you are leaving

Rewrite every sentence about what you are leaving as a sentence about where you are going. Your reasons are valid, and productivity targets and Sunday documentation come up again and again in the threads. Retention doubt is still one of the four reasons career changers get rejected. A letter that says "I am exhausted by clinical work" reads to a hiring manager as a person running, and people who run once tend to run again.
Build the letter in four beats and about 250 words

items.label: Open
items.note: the role, the pivot without apology, your bridge claim and a number

items.label: Map
items.note: two or three accomplishments tied to their first-90-days problems

items.label: Pull
items.note: where you are heading, and proof you have already invested

items.label: Close
items.note: two warm sentences that look forward, with no groveling

blocks.text: Skip "I am writing to express my interest", because they know what a cover letter is. For the map, read the posting the way you read a chart: what is going wrong here, and which of your numbers speaks to it? The pull answers the retention doubt without you ever promising to stay.

blocks.title: The skeleton, with the parts you fill in
blocks.text:
Dear [name, if the posting or LinkedIn gives you one],

I'm applying for [role] at [company]. I'm a speech-language pathologist moving into [function], and I've been doing [function] my whole career under a different job title: [one sentence with a number, e.g. 62 client accounts at a time, each with goals, a timeline and a quarterly review].

Your posting says [requirement quoted or paraphrased in their words]. In my last role I [accomplishment, with the number and the change]. It also says [second requirement]. That's the work I did when [second accomplishment, with the number and the change].

[The paragraph only you could write: the specific thing about this company, this product or the people they serve, and what it made you think. One or two sentences of what you have already done to prepare: the artifact, the course, the three conversations.]

I'd welcome the chance to talk about [the first-90-days problem you named above].

[Your name]

blocks.title: The opening, before and after
blocks.before: Dear Hiring Manager, I am writing to express my interest in the Implementation Specialist position at your organization. As a dedicated Speech-Language Pathologist with over [8] years of experience, I believe my strong communication skills make me an ideal candidate.
blocks.after: I'm applying for the Implementation Specialist role, and I've been doing customer success my whole career. I just called it patient and family care: [62] accounts at a time, quarterly reviews with families who did not always want to hear the data, and [90] percent of them still with me a year later.

blocks.text: Write one paragraph no other applicant could send

One paragraph in the middle has to be impossible to paste into another letter: a product you have used with a real client, a specific thing about who the company serves, a question their pricing page raised for you. SLPs applying to speech-tech and AAC companies have an advantage here and rarely use it. You have put their device in a child's hands, or explained their platform to a family on a Tuesday afternoon. No other applicant in that pile can write the sentence that starts with what happened next.
Check yours against a finished letter for a customer success role

This letter fills in the skeleton for a customer success role at a teletherapy platform, with the numbers left as brackets because yours are different. Test every sentence the same way: if any SLP could have written it, rewrite it.

blocks.title: Customer success, teletherapy platform
blocks.text:
I'm an SLP with eight years in schools, the last three of them as the person who onboarded every new family and every new teacher onto [the platform we used], and I'd like to do that work for [Company] full time.

I've used [Company's product] with [N] students and I know where families get stuck in the first two weeks, because I was the one they called.

Three things from the posting I've already done. I trained [N] teachers and aides on a new documentation system in one semester. I kept a caseload of [N] families engaged through a remote year, with [N] percent still attending in May. And I built the home-program handouts my district still sends out.

I'm moving from clinical work into customer success because the part of the job I'd keep is the onboarding, and here it's the whole job. My résumé is attached, and I'd welcome a conversation.

[Your name]

items.q: Your draft opens "After eight years of unmanageable caseloads, I am ready for a change." What do you do with that sentence?
options: Keep it, because honesty builds trust.
Replace it with the role, the pivot and one number about the work you want more of.
Soften it to "seeking new challenges".
items.why: A sentence about what you are leaving feeds the retention doubt, and a sentence about where you are going answers it.

items.q: The form says a cover letter is optional. You are an SLP applying for an onboarding role. What do you send?
options: Nothing, since recruiters skip them.
Last week's letter with the company name changed.
A short letter with one paragraph only you could write about this company.
items.why: The letter is the one place you can explain the change, and it only works when it could not go to another company.

items: Write the letter once, this week, for the posting you are going to send in 4.7.
Delete every sentence that could survive a copy and paste into another company's letter.
Read it aloud, then send the shorter version.

takeaways: A cover letter reads as proof of effort spent on this company specifically, which is why generic ones fail even when they are well written.
Rewrite every sentence about what you are leaving into a sentence about where you are going, because retention doubt is doing the rejecting.
Four beats: open with the pivot and a number, map two accomplishments to first-90-days problems, name the pull with your proof of investment, close short.
One middle paragraph must be impossible to paste into any other letter.
Delete anything portable, then send the shorter version.

tldr: One application, done properly: a posting under 48 hours old, a résumé tailored to its actual requirement lines, a letter with one paragraph nobody else could write, ten minutes spent finding a human, and a row in the tracker.

blocks.text: Apply while the posting is new

Early applications are the ones most likely to be read. Recruiters often start reviewing as applications arrive, and by the end of the first week they are triaging a pile. One application sent inside 48 hours is worth more than five sent the following Sunday, which is when most of us batch them, because Sunday is when the dread arrives and the laptop is already open. A strong fit that is a week old is still worth sending.
Find one person at the company before you submit

Referrals are behind most of the documented transitions, and generic applications with nobody attached to them are what the failed attempts have in common. Spend ten minutes looking for one person with your target title at that company, or better, an SLP who already works there, and send them the first message from 3.2. Then apply without waiting for the reply.
Decide your answers to the form's knockout questions before you open it

The form after the résumé upload is where automatic screening does happen, and a false answer on it is easy to discover and hard to recover from. For the salary box, know two numbers before you start: the documented range for your path, and where you sit now. The profession's median is $97,870, and its middle half runs $77,730 to $114,570.

items.title: Years of experience
items.text: Answer honestly. Where the form allows a sentence, describe the function you did as well as the title you held.

items.title: Licenses and work authorization
items.text: Answer exactly. If a requirement you cannot meet is a true hard no, send a different posting this week.

items.title: Salary
items.text: If the posting shows a pay range, answer inside it. Otherwise answer from the documented range for your path.

blocks.text: Send one application properly, in this order

items: Pick one posting for your path that went up in the last 48 hours.
Copy its requirement lines into a list and mark every one you have evidence for. The unmarked ones wait for Module 5.
Tailor the summary and the top three bullets under your most recent role to those lines, using the posting's own words and keeping your numbers.
Write the letter with the 4.6 skeleton, including the one paragraph nobody else could write.
Spend ten minutes finding one person at the company and send them the first message from 3.2.
Submit, then log it in the tracker with the posting date, so the next month becomes a set of numbers instead of a feeling.

items.label: the window to aim for, while the pile is still small
one documented transition: tailored applications, interviews, offer
the typical documented timeline, with some at 1.5 to 2.5 years

blocks.text: Expect silence after your first ten applications
hire a resume writer who specializes in career changes and keep at it. It took me two years.

Silence after ten applications tells you almost nothing, because the documented ratios are large. One transition took 113 tailored applications to produce 7 interviews and 1 offer. A data analyst sent more than 500 over six months and now works remotely for more than their SLP salary. Track the count, set a weekly number you can hit while working full time, and judge the search by the month.

items.q: On a Tuesday night you find a posting that fits, six hours old. Your résumé still needs tailoring. What do you do?
options: Save it for Sunday and send it with four others.
Tailor the summary and top three bullets, find one person, and send it inside 48 hours.
Send the untailored résumé tonight to be first in the pile.
items.why: Early applications are the most likely to be read, and the reader still has to map your top bullets onto the posting.

items.q: A form makes expected salary a required number, and the posting shows no range. What goes in the box?
options: Your current clinical salary.
Zero, to keep the conversation open.
A number from the documented range for your path, decided before you opened the form.
items.why: The salary box is a knockout question, and the documented range for your path is the answer you prepared for it.

takeaways: Applications in the first day or two of a posting are the most likely to be read, so one sent early beats five sent in a Sunday batch.
Referrals are behind most documented transitions, so spend ten minutes finding one human before you submit.
Knockout questions on the form are the real automatic filter, and the salary box wants a number you decided in advance.
Tailor to the requirement lines in the posting's own words, and leave the gaps for Module 5.
